body.html: The abdomen contains intraperitoneal and retroperitoneal organs within a wall of overlapping muscle and connective tissue: the anterolateral wall, the inguinal canal and the posterior wall. The wall protects the viscera, maintains their position, helps raise abdominal pressure (coughing, defecation, childbirth) and moves the trunk. The slides are mostly labelled images; this page gives the anatomy they illustrate.

Rule of 3 (lateral to rectus): 3 layers above the muscles (skin, fatty Camper's fascia, membranous Scarpa's fascia), 3 flat muscles (external oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis) and 3 layers below (transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, parietal peritoneum). The external oblique's lower edge forms the inguinal ligament and its aponeurosis the superficial (external) inguinal ring. The internal oblique gives the cremaster muscle along the spermatic cord and, with transversus, the conjoint tendon. Vertical muscles: rectus abdominis (bounded laterally by the linea semilunaris) and the small pyramidalis. The flat muscles' aponeuroses form the rectus sheath and meet at the linea alba; below the arcuate line the posterior sheath is missing and only transversalis fascia lies behind rectus. Umbilicus: umbilical vein → round ligament of the liver; urachus → median umbilical ligament; umbilical arteries → medial umbilical ligaments. Lymph: superficially, above the umbilicus to axillary nodes and below it to superficial inguinal nodes; deeply to internal thoracic, lumbar and external iliac nodes. Weak areas: umbilicus (umbilical hernia), linea semilunaris (Spigelian hernia), surgical incisions.

An oblique passage (about 4 cm) above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, formed during the descent of the testis. It runs from the deep ring (opening in the transversalis fascia, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels) to the superficial ring (in the external oblique aponeurosis, above the pubic tubercle). Walls: anterior, external oblique aponeurosis (+ internal oblique laterally); posterior, transversalis fascia (+ conjoint tendon medially); roof, arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus; floor, inguinal ligament (+ lacunar ligament medially). Contents: spermatic cord in males, round ligament of the uterus in females, plus the ilio-inguinal nerve and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. Indirect inguinal hernias enter the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; direct hernias push through the posterior wall medial to them.

Bones: lumbar vertebrae, sacrum, pelvic bones, ribs 11-12. Muscles: medially psoas major (and minor), laterally quadratus lumborum, inferiorly iliacus (joins psoas as iliopsoas, the main hip flexor), superiorly the diaphragm.

The biliary system is a network of ducts that transports, stores and releases bile, crossing the liver, porta hepatis, hepatoduodenal ligament, pancreas and major duodenal papilla. Bile (water, electrolytes, bile acids, cholesterol, phospholipids and pigments, mainly bilirubin from haemoglobin breakdown) is made continuously by the liver, 600-1000 mL/day, stored and concentrated in the gallbladder and released when food, especially fat, enters the duodenum. Bile salts are reabsorbed in the ileum and return to the liver via the portal vein: the enterohepatic circulation.

Intrahepatic ducts follow the functional segments, running in the portal triads within Glisson's capsule (subsegmental → segmental → sectoral ducts); anatomical variants are frequent and create injury risk in liver surgery and cholecystectomy. At the hilum, the right and left hepatic ducts join (the biliary confluence) over the origin of the right portal vein, in front of and above the right hepatic artery, within the hilar plate (connective tissue fused with Glisson's capsule). The right duct is short; the left duct has a long extrahepatic course under the quadrate lobe, which surgeons use for repairs. Perihilar cholangiocarcinoma affects this confluence.

The common hepatic duct runs in the hepatoduodenal ligament and joins the cystic duct to form the common bile duct, which passes behind the duodenum and through the head of the pancreas to the hepatopancreatic ampulla, opening into the descending duodenum at the major duodenal papilla, controlled by the sphincter of Oddi (accessible by endoscopy: stone extraction, sphincterotomy). The gallbladder is a pear-shaped sac under segments 4b-5, above the first part of the duodenum, with a fundus, body and neck; the cystic duct contains the spiral valve of Heister. The hepatocystic triangle (liver, cystic duct, common hepatic duct), crossed by the cystic artery (related to Calot's triangle), must be dissected to obtain the critical view of safety before clipping anything in a cholecystectomy.

Arteries: intrahepatic ducts and confluence from the right and left hepatic arteries; main bile duct from the right hepatic, gastroduodenal and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries; gallbladder and cystic duct from the cystic artery. Nerves: sympathetic (coeliac plexus: bile storage, visceral pain), parasympathetic (vagal trunks: bile release), and the right phrenic nerve to Glisson's capsule (somatic pain, referred to the right shoulder). Lymph: cystic → hepatic → coeliac nodes, and pyloric → peripancreatic → mesenteric nodes.

The large intestine absorbs water, produces vitamins K and B (bacterial flora), compacts and stores faeces and moves them toward the rectum. Parts: caecum (with appendix), ascending colon, hepatic flexure, transverse colon, splenic flexure, descending colon, sigmoid colon, then rectum. Clinical: endoscopic exploration, colon cancer, appendicitis.

Features unique to the colon: taeniae coli (three bands of longitudinal muscle), haustra (sacculations) and omental (epiploic) appendices (fat tags). Wall: mucosa, submucosa, inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle, serosa. Caecum: usually in the right iliac fossa (75%), sometimes pelvic or subhepatic; intraperitoneal; lies on the iliacus, with the ileum and appendix medially. Appendix: blind diverticulum 6-10 cm long, whose base is on the posteromedial caecum below the ileocaecal junction, where the three taeniae converge (surgical landmark); vessels run in the mesoappendix; the base projects at McBurney's point, but the tip position varies, so appendicitis pain can be felt in different places. Ascending colon (right flank; about 10 cm, 6 cm wide) to the hepatic flexure; transverse colon, mobile on the transverse mesocolon; descending colon (left flank; about 25 cm, 4 cm wide), from the splenic flexure, fixed to the posterior wall; sigmoid colon (about 40 cm, 3 cm wide), mobile on the sigmoid mesocolon, whose root lies over the left ureter, related to the pouch of Douglas and, in women, the ovary.

Superior mesenteric artery (midgut): ileocolic (caecum, appendix), right colic (ascending colon), middle colic (transverse colon). Inferior mesenteric artery (hindgut): left colic, sigmoid arteries and superior rectal artery. The marginal artery links them along the colon. Veins follow the arteries into the superior and inferior mesenteric veins, then the portal vein. Lymph passes through a chain of nodes: epicolic (on the wall) → paracolic → intermediate (ileocolic, mesocolic, sigmoid) → main (superior and inferior mesenteric) nodes, which is why colon cancer surgery removes the colon with its mesentery and vessels.

The liver is the largest abdominal organ (about 2% of adult body weight, 4-5% in infants), wedge-shaped and reddish brown, a vital organ for homeostasis, nutrition and defence (detoxification, protein synthesis, bile production, glycogen storage). Its 'hidden' anatomy has a double inflow (portal vein and hepatic artery) and a double outflow (hepatic veins and bile ducts).

It lies mostly in the right hypochondrium (about three quarters) and extends into the epigastrium and left hypochondrium. Surface markings (neutral breathing): superior border from the 5th right rib to the 6th left rib via the xiphisternal junction; inferior border from the 10th right costal cartilage to the 6th left rib (may be palpable in healthy adults); it moves with breathing (risk of pneumothorax during liver puncture). Surfaces: diaphragmatic (under the domes; above lie the right lung and heart); visceral/inferior (gallbladder, porta hepatis, lesser omentum; impressions of oesophagus, stomach, duodenum, right colic flexure, right kidney and adrenal); posterior with the bare area (not covered by peritoneum, bounded by the coronary ligaments) and the groove of the inferior vena cava. Subphrenic and hepatorenal recesses collect fluid, blood or abscesses.

Six peritoneal 'ligaments': falciform (to the anterior wall), round ligament (ligamentum teres), remnant of the umbilical vein, coronary and right and left triangular ligaments (to the diaphragm), the lesser omentum (to the lesser curvature), and the ligamentum venosum, remnant of the ductus venosus. Anatomical lobes (external appearance): right, left (divided by the falciform ligament), quadrate (between gallbladder and ligamentum teres, part of the right lobe) and caudate (between IVC and ligamentum venosum). The hepatoduodenal ligament carries the portal triad (portal vein, hepatic artery, bile duct) to the porta hepatis (hilum); behind it lies the omental foramen; clamping it (Pringle manoeuvre) stops liver inflow. The portal vein brings digestive blood (nutrients, but also bacteria and tumour cells: abscesses, metastases) between two capillary beds. Portosystemic anastomoses: oesophageal, paraumbilical (caput medusae), rectal and retroperitoneal; in portal hypertension they dilate and varices can bleed. Hepatic artery variants are common.

The functional (Couinaud) division, based on independent inflow, drainage and bile outflow, is used in surgery: 2 hemilivers (separated by the main portal fissure, plane of the middle hepatic vein), 4 sectors and 8 segments (1 = caudate; 2-4 left; 5-8 right), each with its own Glissonian pedicle. The three hepatic veins (right, middle, left) join the IVC at the hepatocaval confluence. Nerves: hepatic plexus with sympathetic fibres (coeliac and superior mesenteric plexuses) and parasympathetic fibres (vagal trunks); lower intercostal nerves supply Glisson's capsule. Lymph: parenchymal and subperitoneal systems, mainly caudally to abdominal nodes and cranially to mediastinal nodes.

A network of vessels and nodes carrying lymph (fluid with immune cells, proteins and fats) alongside the circulation. Functions: fluid balance (returns interstitial fluid), immune surveillance (filters pathogens and cancer cells), fat absorption (chylomicrons via lacteals to the thoracic duct). Knowing its routes explains the spread of infection and cancer, guides oncological surgery (lymphadenectomy in gastric or colorectal cancer), imaging interpretation, the sentinel node concept and chylous ascites after lymphatic injury. Lymph flows centrally and ends in the thoracic duct, which empties into the left subclavian vein.

Parietal lymphatics drain the wall and follow the veins: superficially, above the umbilicus to axillary and below it to superficial inguinal nodes; deeply to external iliac, common iliac and lumbar (para-aortic) nodes. Visceral lymphatics drain the organs and follow the arteries to the pre-aortic nodes: foregut → coeliac, midgut → superior mesenteric, hindgut → inferior mesenteric nodes. The lumbar trunks converge in front of L1-L2 into the cisterna chyli (a fusiform sac about 5-7 cm long), which continues, right of the aorta, as the thoracic duct at about T12. Organs: oesophagus (longitudinal submucosal network allowing spread up and down): upper third → deep cervical, middle → mediastinal, lower → left gastric and coeliac nodes; liver: parenchymal and subperitoneal systems, mainly to abdominal and mediastinal nodes; biliary tree: cystic → hepatic → coeliac and pyloric → peripancreatic nodes.

Thoracoabdominal nerves (T7-T11), continuations of the lower intercostals: skin and muscles of the anterolateral wall; subcostal nerve (T12); iliohypogastric (L1): suprapubic skin, internal oblique and transversus; ilio-inguinal (L1): passes through the inguinal canal; upper medial thigh, mons pubis, scrotum or labia majora; genitofemoral (L1-L2): genital branch to the cremaster and scrotal/labial skin, femoral branch to the upper anterior thigh. These guide incisions and fascial plane blocks.

The autonomic system has sympathetic, parasympathetic and enteric divisions. Sympathetic (preganglionic neurons T5-L2): greater splanchnic (T5-T9) → coeliac ganglion, lesser (T10-T11) → superior mesenteric ganglion, least (T12) → aorticorenal ganglion, lumbar splanchnics (L1-L2) → inferior mesenteric ganglion and hypogastric plexuses; effects: inhibits peristalsis, contracts sphincters, vasoconstriction. Parasympathetic: vagus to the foregut and midgut up to the proximal two thirds of the transverse colon; pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) to the hindgut, bladder and reproductive organs; synapse in intramural ganglia; effects: stimulates peristalsis and secretion, relaxes sphincters, enables urination, defecation and sexual function. Pelvic surgery (rectal resection, hysterectomy) can injure these plexuses (urinary retention, sexual dysfunction). The enteric nervous system ('second brain') has the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus between the muscle layers (motility) and the submucosal (Meissner) plexus (secretion, local blood flow).

A soft, leaf-shaped, elongated gland 12-20 cm long with a thin capsule, retroperitoneal, lying behind the lesser sac, in front of L1-L2, between the duodenum (right) and the spleen (left). It is both exocrine (acinar cells → pancreatic juice) and endocrine (islets → insulin and glucagon).

Five parts. Head: in the C-curve of the duodenum, right of the superior mesenteric vessels, on the IVC and left renal vein; the bile duct runs in a groove on its posterosuperior surface. Uncinate process: projects medially behind the SMA and SMV. Neck: short, lies over the portal vein, formed behind it by the union of the SMV and splenic vein. Body: left of the superior mesenteric vessels, crosses the aorta and L2 just above the transpyloric plane; its front, covered by peritoneum, forms the floor of the lesser sac and the stomach bed; behind are the aorta, left adrenal, left kidney and renal vessels. Tail: mobile, runs in the splenorenal ligament with the splenic vessels to the splenic hilum, near the left colic flexure.

The main duct forms by fusion of the ventral and dorsal bud ducts. The main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) runs from tail to head and joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater), opening at the major duodenal papilla in D2. Smooth-muscle sphincters (of the pancreatic duct, of the bile duct, and the sphincter of Oddi) regulate secretion under autonomic control. The accessory duct (of Santorini) drains the head and uncinate process and opens at the minor papilla. Variants: annular pancreas (ventral bud rotation failure, ring around D2) and pancreas divisum (no communication; the dorsal duct drains most of the gland via the minor papilla).

Double arterial supply. Head, neck and uncinate process: anterior and posterior superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (from the gastroduodenal, coeliac territory) anastomosing with the inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (from the SMA) in arcades; these arcades can supply the liver when the coeliac trunk is compressed (median arcuate ligament syndrome). Body and tail: branches of the splenic artery (dorsal pancreatic, greater pancreatic, artery to the tail). Veins: head → SMV and portal vein; body and tail → splenic vein. Lymph follows the arteries to coeliac and superior mesenteric nodes.

The bony pelvis (two hip bones, sacrum, coccyx) has an inlet (sacral promontory → iliopectineal line → pubic symphysis) and an outlet (coccyx → ischial tuberosities → pubic arch). The greater (false) pelvis lies above the brim; the lesser (true) pelvis below it contains the rectum, bladder, uterus or prostate and gonads, closed by the pelvic floor (levator ani and coccygeus). The aorta bifurcates at L4 (umbilicus, iliac crest level), giving the small median sacral artery; each common iliac artery divides at the sacroiliac joint (L5/S1) into the external iliac (under the inguinal ligament → femoral artery) and the internal iliac (pelvis, perineum).

About 4 cm, divides into two divisions. Anterior (visceral + some parietal): superior vesical (from the umbilical artery, which after birth obliterates into the medial umbilical ligament; bladder dome, distal ureter); inferior vesical in males (bladder base, seminal vesicles, prostate) or vaginal in females; uterine artery, which runs medially in the base of the broad ligament and crosses over the ureter ('water under the bridge') to reach the cervix, then ascends tortuously; middle rectal (middle third of rectum; anastomoses with superior rectal from the IMA and inferior rectal from the pudendal); obturator (through the obturator canal to the medial thigh and hip); internal pudendal (leaves through the greater sciatic foramen, hooks around the ischial spine, re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen: inferior rectal, perineal and penile/clitoral arteries); inferior gluteal. Posterior (parietal only): iliolumbar, lateral sacral, superior gluteal.

The internal iliac vein joins the external iliac vein to form the common iliac vein at L5/S1; the left common iliac vein is longer and crosses under the right common iliac artery (compression can cause left-sided DVT). Large venous plexuses: vesical, prostatic (receives the deep dorsal vein of the penis), uterine, vaginal, sacral and rectal (superior rectal → IMV → portal; middle and inferior rectal → internal iliac → systemic: a portosystemic anastomosis). Lymph nodes: external iliac (bladder, prostate/cervix, lower limb via inguinal), internal iliac (all pelvic viscera, perineum), obturator (prostate, bladder neck, cervix: key for staging prostate and cervical cancer), presacral (rectum, posterior organs) → common iliac → para-aortic nodes.

Sympathetic (T10-L2): lumbar splanchnics → inferior mesenteric ganglion → superior hypogastric plexus (in front of L5/S1, between the common iliac arteries, purely sympathetic) → right and left hypogastric nerves → inferior hypogastric (pelvic) plexus. Functions: storage and ejaculation: relaxes the detrusor, closes the bladder neck, contracts the internal anal sphincter, vasoconstriction. Parasympathetic: pelvic splanchnic nerves (nervi erigentes), S2-S4, leave via the anterior sacral foramina to join the inferior hypogastric plexus. Functions: emptying and erection: detrusor contraction (micturition), rectal contraction (defecation), vasodilation, glandular secretion. The inferior hypogastric plexus, on the lateral pelvic walls, gives vesical, rectal, prostatic (with cavernous nerves) and uterovaginal (Frankenhäuser) plexuses. Micturition: filling needs sympathetic tone and pudendal control of the external sphincter; voiding needs parasympathetic detrusor contraction. Lesions above S2 give a spastic bladder; lesions of S2-S4 give a flaccid bladder with overflow incontinence. Defecation: internal anal sphincter (smooth, involuntary, sympathetic) and external sphincter (skeletal, pudendal nerve); the rectoanal inhibitory reflex relaxes the internal sphincter.

The pelvic floor separates the pelvic cavity from the perineum and is formed by muscles and fascia: the levator ani and coccygeus. The perineum is the region of soft tissues below the pelvic diaphragm. Functions: support of the pelvic organs, control of urination and defecation, and sexual function. Clinical relevance: examination, pelvic organ prolapse and incontinence. Much of the lecture is labelled figures; this page summarises them.

The diamond-shaped perineum, bounded by the pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments and coccyx, is divided by a line between the ischial tuberosities into the anterior urogenital triangle and the posterior anal triangle. External landmarks in females include the clitoral hood and glans, external urethral orifice, labia majora and minora, vaginal opening and hymen, and the anus. The urogenital perineum has layers: cutaneous plane, superficial perineal space (below the inferior fascia of the urogenital diaphragm, the perineal membrane) containing the ischiocavernosus, bulbospongiosus and superficial transverse perineal muscles with the erectile tissue (corpora cavernosa and spongiosum or clitoris and vestibular bulbs) and the greater vestibular glands; and the deep perineal space containing the external urethral sphincter (compressor urethrae and urethrovaginal sphincter in females) and the deep transverse perineal muscle, with the bulbourethral glands in males. The anal triangle contains the anal canal, external anal sphincter and ischioanal fossae. The perineal body is the central fibromuscular point where these muscles converge.

The levator ani has three parts: puborectalis (a sling around the anorectal junction that maintains the anorectal angle, key for faecal continence), pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus; with the coccygeus it forms the pelvic diaphragm, supporting the bladder, uterus and rectum and resisting rises in abdominal pressure. It is supplied mainly by branches of S3-S4 and the pudendal nerve. Childbirth trauma, ageing and chronic straining weaken these structures, leading to pelvic organ prolapse (bladder, uterus or rectum descending) and urinary or faecal incontinence; pelvic floor exercises strengthen them.

The small intestine is the longest part of the GI tract (about 6-7 m), filling most of the abdomen from the pylorus to the ileocaecal junction. Its roles are digestion, absorption and motility. Three parts: duodenum (20-30 cm), jejunum (about 2.5 m, two fifths) and ileum (about 3.5 m, three fifths). Surface area is multiplied by plicae circulares, villi and microvilli. Wall: mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa; special cells: enterocytes, goblet cells, Paneth cells (antimicrobial) and enteroendocrine cells.

C-shaped, 20-25 cm, curving around the head of the pancreas; mostly retroperitoneal (except its first part), the site of chemical digestion: gastric chyme is neutralised and mixed with bile and pancreatic juice. Four parts: 1st (superior), with the mobile, intraperitoneal duodenal cap; 2nd (descending), receiving the bile and pancreatic ducts at the major duodenal papilla; 3rd (horizontal), crossed in front by the superior mesenteric vessels; 4th (ascending), ending at the duodenojejunal flexure, held by the ligament of Treitz (suspensory ligament of the duodenum). Its blood supply comes from the coeliac trunk (superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries via the gastroduodenal) and the SMA (inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries), reflecting the foregut-midgut junction. Brunner's glands in the submucosa are typical of the duodenum.

The jejunum is wider, thicker and more vascular, with tall plicae; the ileum is narrower, with Peyer's patches, and ends at the ileocaecal junction. Both are intraperitoneal, suspended by the mesentery, whose root runs obliquely on the posterior wall and carries the vessels, nerves and lymphatics. Arteries: 15-18 jejunal and ileal branches of the SMA form anastomotic loops (arcades) that give straight vasa recta to the wall (long with few arcades in the jejunum; short with many arcades in the ileum). Veins join the superior mesenteric vein → portal vein. Clinical: mesenteric infarction, obstruction (dilated loops on imaging), coeliac disease, Crohn's disease.

An ovoid, soft, purplish, pulpy organ with a thin capsule, normally 10-12 cm and 150-200 g in adults (very variable). It is intraperitoneal, suspended by peritoneal folds; only the hilum is bare. It is the largest mass of lymphoid tissue: lymphocyte proliferation, immune surveillance and defence.

In the superolateral left hypochondrium, protected by the lower thoracic cage and not normally descending below the costal margin (a palpable spleen is abnormal); it moves with breathing. It lies against the left 9th-11th ribs, its long axis parallel to the 10th rib, separated from them by the diaphragm and the costodiaphragmatic recess (so rib fractures can injure lung, pleura and spleen). Two surfaces: diaphragmatic (related to the recess and lower left lung) and visceral (left colic flexure, pancreatic tail, stomach, kidney), with the hilum transmitting splenic vessels, nerves and lymphatics. Two borders (superior, notched; inferior) and two extremities (posterior and anterior poles).

Seven peritoneal ligaments: gastrosplenic (short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels), splenophrenic, splenorenal (splenic vessels and tail of the pancreas), pancreaticosplenic, pancreaticocolic (mesocolon), splenocolic and phrenicocolic (parts of the greater omentum).

The splenic artery, the largest branch of the coeliac trunk, runs a tortuous course along the upper border of the pancreas, behind the lesser sac and in front of the left kidney, then in the splenorenal ligament, dividing into 2-3 branches before the hilum. Its segmental branching allows partial (segmental) splenectomy and distal pancreatectomy with spleen preservation. The splenic vein leaves the hilum, runs behind the pancreas and joins the SMV to form the portal vein (splenic vein thrombosis causes gastric varices). Lymph goes to coeliac and superior mesenteric nodes; nerves come from the vagus and splanchnic nerves. Splenectomy (emergency after trauma or elective) leaves patients vulnerable to encapsulated bacteria.

A muscular tube about 25 cm long carrying food from the pharynx to the stomach by peristalsis (a conduit only, no digestion). It begins at C6 (cricoid cartilage), crosses the diaphragm at the oesophageal hiatus (T10) and joins the stomach at about T11. Two sphincters: the upper (prevents air entry) and the lower (LES) (prevents reflux). Clinical: GERD (LES dysfunction, heartburn), achalasia (LES fails to relax), oesophageal cancer. Wall: mucosa (non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium), submucosa with mucous glands, muscularis (upper third skeletal, middle mixed, lower third smooth), and adventitia (no serosa). Relations: cervical part: trachea and recurrent laryngeal nerves in front, carotids and thyroid laterally; thoracic part (posterior mediastinum): trachea then left atrium in front, vertebrae, thoracic duct and azygos behind, aortic arch and thoracic aorta on the left; abdominal part: left lobe of the liver in front, left crus behind. Arteries: inferior thyroid (cervical), aortic and bronchial branches (thoracic), left gastric (abdominal). Veins: inferior thyroid, azygos/hemiazygos, and the left gastric vein → portal vein: a key portosystemic anastomosis (oesophageal varices in portal hypertension).

A J-shaped organ in the upper left quadrant between oesophagus and duodenum; regions: cardia, fundus, body, pylorus; lesser and greater curvatures; four wall layers (mucosa, submucosa, muscularis externa, serosa). It is intraperitoneal. Lesser omentum (from the lesser curvature and first part of duodenum to the liver): hepatogastric and hepatoduodenal ligaments; the latter contains the portal triad and forms the front of the epiploic foramen (of Winslow), connecting greater and lesser sacs; compressing it (Pringle manoeuvre) controls liver bleeding. Greater omentum (from the greater curvature): gastrocolic, gastrosplenic (short gastric vessels) and gastrophrenic ligaments. The lesser sac lies behind the stomach, in front of the pancreas, left kidney and adrenal.

Arteries (all from the coeliac trunk): lesser curvature: left gastric (coeliac) and right gastric (common hepatic); greater curvature: left gastroepiploic (splenic) and right gastroepiploic (gastroduodenal); fundus: short gastric arteries (splenic). Veins parallel the arteries into the portal system: left gastric → portal vein; short gastrics and left gastroepiploic → splenic vein; right gastroepiploic → superior mesenteric vein. Nerves: parasympathetic vagus (stimulates secretion and motility), sympathetic from the coeliac plexus (inhibits). Peptic ulcer (gastric or duodenal): mainly Helicobacter pylori and NSAIDs; complications include bleeding and perforation. Gastric cancer is another key pathology.

The abdominal aorta continues the thoracic aorta at the diaphragm (T12) and ends by bifurcating into the common iliac arteries at L4. Its branches are anterior, lateral and posterior, paired or unpaired. Anterior unpaired branches (digestive tract): coeliac trunk (T12), foregut: left gastric (stomach, lower oesophagus), common hepatic (liver, gallbladder, pancreas, part of duodenum; gives the gastroduodenal artery), splenic (spleen, pancreas, stomach); superior mesenteric artery (L1), midgut: small intestine except the duodenum, caecum, appendix, ascending colon and part of the transverse colon, via inferior pancreaticoduodenal, jejunal and ileal, ileocolic, right colic and middle colic arteries; inferior mesenteric artery (L3), hindgut: descending and sigmoid colon, rectum, via left colic, sigmoid and superior rectal arteries. Coeliac trunk variants are common. Gonadal arteries (testicular or ovarian) arise below the renal arteries and run down on psoas (to the deep inguinal ring, or the suspensory ligament of the ovary). Lateral branches: middle suprarenal, renal (just below the SMA, L1-L2: kidneys, adrenals, ureters). Posterior branches: inferior phrenic and lumbar arteries (at risk in aortic surgery). Abdominal aortic aneurysm is treated by open repair or endovascular stent graft.

Returns blood from everything below the diaphragm to the right atrium. It forms by the union of the common iliac veins at L5, ascends to the right of the aorta, and passes through the central tendon of the diaphragm at T8. It is crossed in front by the right common iliac artery, right gonadal artery, duodenum, pancreatic head, bile duct, portal vein and liver. Tributaries: common iliac, lumbar, gonadal (right into the IVC; left into the left renal vein), renal, right suprarenal, inferior phrenic and hepatic veins, but none from the digestive tract or spleen, which drain via the portal vein. Lumbar and azygos veins provide inferior-to-superior and left-to-right shunts. Leg and pelvic deep vein thrombosis can embolise via the IVC to the lungs.

The portal vein collects blood from the digestive tract and spleen and carries it to the liver sinusoids, linking two capillary systems. Tributaries: superior mesenteric vein, splenic vein (receiving the inferior mesenteric vein), left and right gastric veins. Portosystemic anastomoses: oesophageal, paraumbilical, rectal and retroperitoneal. In portal hypertension they dilate (oesophageal varices, caput medusae, rectal varices); treatments include TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) and surgical shunts.
